utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, sir. May I just remind you that at the beginning of your testimony you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, nothing else but the truth. I just remind you that you are still bound by that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't know whether I should let you speak or should I speak before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We got the news. We're terribly sorry. May his soul rest in peace. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Should I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the point you were going to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, I was just going to continue with the cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I know that following on from Monday there was a discussion and the Prosecution filed a written response on the issue of further evidence, but I'll just wait until the Court brings that up. I can continue in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dakic.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to continue with my questions now for a while. On Monday where we left off was we were talking about the period around July and August of 1990, so I'm going to take up there again. And actually, it would be great if you could have a copy of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If the registrar and the usher could provide the witness with a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, this way you'll be able to follow along as I -- and I'll point you to specific paragraphs as much as I can. And my first question or two will be in regards to paragraph 21, where you discuss the seizure of reserve police weapons. And you say there that the Croatian MUP began taking away reserve police weapons "in all Serb municipalities on the territories of Northern Dalmatia and Lika." Sir, in fact what happened was the reserve police weapons were seized only in Benkovac. There may have been an attempt to seize them in Obrovac but it failed, and there were no other places where the Croatian MUP seized reserve police weapons in August 1990, at least in that area that you referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is a fact that the Croatian police was not able to seize weapons everywhere because the police sided with the people in many areas and they were unable to see this through. But there was the intention to seize weapons in all the Serb-inhabited areas while at the same time the HDZ was arming its members. We knew where this was all going. We know that in Glina the Croatian police occupied the local police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm -- it's correct, isn't it, that it was only in Benkovac where the reserve police weapons were actually seized, not in all Serb municipalities, as you put it in your statement, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention was evident, and that was to seize weapons in all the Serb municipalities. But they were unable to pull this through because the police station -- some of the police stations sided with the local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, that's not -- sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript says the Croatian police began taking away arms and weapons placed at police station warehouses in all Serb municipalities. So what I said was that it began seizing weapons; I did not say that it seized weapons in all these municipalities. I stand by what I said in my statement. And there is this well-known incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where a helicopter was returned to the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We've heard about that well-known incident from other witnesses, so you don't need to address it. But you didn't talk about -- in your statement about intentions. What you said was they began with taking away the weapons; in fact, that's not true. Only in Benkovac were weapons taken away or seized and nowhere else, right, in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact information as to where weapons were taken. I know that they began the process, that there -- the intention was there, and I stand by my statement that this was indeed their intention --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, I was at the head of the Petrova Gora museum and we had weapons. And the Karlovac police force came to take the weapons. I told them that the weapons stored in the museum were not workable and that they could not be used. Therefore, they tried to seize all the weapons that existed in the Serb-inhabited areas. This crime was long in the making. We anticipated what was to happen. We suffered a genocide, a pure genocide in World War II. In my area where I hailed from, one out of three people were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. We don't need to hear about World War II. I'm focused on the 1990s. When was it that you say that this happened that the Karlovac police came and tried to seize weapons from the Petrova Gora memorial? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it happened toward the end of 1990. They came to bring me into -- before the Karlovac court because I wrote a satirical poem about Tudjman and they wanted to charge me for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, thanks for the date. That's what I had asked you about. You know, in your statement the reason you talk about this is you're trying to make a point about the -- and then you make a point about the purpose of seizing reserve police weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Do you have something before I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Didn't you ask a question now? I think the witness can answer your question and then I can put mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: In your statement when you talk about this, then you start talking about the purpose of seizing these weapons. And it's -- and you talk about the referendum, so it's clear you were talking about August of 1990. And I just want to ask one more time to see if we're clear on that. In August of 1990, only Benkovac had its reserve police weapons seized by the Croatian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, I don't know. I'm not sure that it didn't happen elsewhere, but let's say that this was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Because you don't know of any other place that it happened in August 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at Donji Lapac they were supposed to come and seize weapons, but the people broke into the depot and took the weapons. The president of the Executive Council Milan Djukic went to Zagreb out of protest because in his opinion weapons should not end up in the hands of the people; they had no business having weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe you had a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Dakic. At page 4, line 19, starting from line 19, the Prosecutor asked you a question as to when it was that you say this happened, and "this" refers to the attempt to take weapons from the Karlovac police station -- I beg your pardon, not from the Karlovac police station but from the Petrova Gora memorial; that's what you say. And when the Karlovac police came and tried to seize weapons from the Petrova Gora memorial, you said: I know that it happened toward the end of 1990. They came to bring me in to -- before the Karlovac court charge because I wrote a satirical poem about Tudjman and they wanted to charge me about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are giving us the reason in that answer why they came. They came to try and charge you. This doesn't seem to have anything to do with taking weapons from Petrova Gora. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. But at the same time they told me that I should appear before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. That's what they told you. They didn't say they are coming to take weapons from Petrova Gora; they were coming to get you to appear before the court, and the reason they wanted you to appear before the court is because you had written a satirical poem about Tudjman, based on your own evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was something they told me in passing, as a matter of fact, that I should appear before the court. But the purpose of their arrival there was to seize weapons. The chief of police from Vojnic went along with me to make an inventory of the weapons, to see whether all the weapons were there. We made the inventory. And the man who had come from the Karlovac police station went back to Karlovac and he satisfied himself that indeed the weapons were all still up there. I recall his name, and I mean the name of the policeman who came to Vojnic. His name was Vucnjec [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. That's a new story. That doesn't detract from my questions. My questions were precisely that what you had told us didn't contain what you are telling us now. You may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, at the end of one of your responses just before His Honour asked you these questions you said that Milan Djukic went to Zagreb out of protest - this is in regards to Donji Lapac - because in his opinion weapons should not end up in the hands of the people; they had no business having weapons. You did not share that view, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I misspoke. Not in the hands of the people but in the hands of the individuals he didn't trust. And he abandoned his post out of protest, went to Zagreb, and was subsequently appointed to a senior position within the police force during the war. And after the war he established the Serb National Party in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me focus your attention on paragraph 22 of your statement. And here you say that the aim of the Croatian MUP at this time, in August of 1990, was not only to collect arms of the reserve police but to prevent the Serb referendum which was scheduled for the 19th of August, 1990. Sir, doesn't that seem to you a rather round-about way of preventing a referendum, seizing reserve police weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact this was an opportunity to prevent the referendum from going ahead, but the main purpose was to disarm all Serb municipalities, because this was the area of the Krajina which was known to have been an area where wars were waged throughout -- through history. The people, the local people, felt safer while having these weapons, but I'm sure that this exercise of collecting arms was connected with the referendum. It says here that I went past some barricades and that the barricades were organised by civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that those were mostly civilian rifles that were to be found at these barricades --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, please again just focus on my questions. And sometimes I -- I don't speak right at the end of when you finish speaking, it's because I'm listening to the interpretation. I'm not inviting you to keep going on to another topic. It's just that I need to get the interpretation before I can ask you the next question. So please focus and try to focus your answers on my questions, okay? Thank you. Sir, you alluded to something similar, but let me put this to you: The real purpose of these attempts, unsuccessful except for in Benkovac, to take control of reserve police weapons, the real purpose was simply to establish control over those weapons in municipalities where the authorities felt there was a risk that those weapons would be used against the Croatian government, as subsequently in fact happened in Knin, right? That was the purpose of taking control of these police reserve weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this wasn't the matter of control, but the matter of physically seizing weapons. They could have had control over the weapons by simply listing them and knowing what there was to be found. This was no control. This was seizing of weapons and relocating them to the areas with a Croatian majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't want to spend too much more time on this. But you say it's seizing the weapons. Well, these weapons were weapons that already belonged to the Croatian police, right? They were simply moving their own weapons from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can't be true because there are two equal people in Croatia. They were under the constitution at the time, and you can't speak of weapons being taken from one people and given to others --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this police officer came to Vojnic, he asked that the weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, sir, you must have misunderstood me. I didn't talk about the Croatian people seizing weapons. It was about the fact that these weapons belonged to the Croatian police, to the MUP of Croatia, right, so they already were -- they already belonged to the MUP of Croatia, and the MUP of Croatia was just taking their own weapons to another place, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with what objective? That's my question. What was the actual goal? Well, you can imagine what it was. The main goal was to have the Serb people disarmed and defenceless, and then they would be easy to manipulate. And this is proved by the fact that subsequently genocide was committed on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to another paragraph, 26, of your statement. There you say that the Croatian constitution of December 1990 caused the war by making Serbs a national minority instead of a constituent people. This is something I think you were just referring to. But, sir, isn't it true that before 1990 there had already been confrontations and violence in the Krajina before 1990; correct? Before December 1990, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such instances and confrontations, but I'm not sure what sort of violence you're referring to. Still, there was no war. One could not even imagine that there would be a war. The people in Krajina did not think about waging a war; we thought about securing our rights. The -- the amendments to the constitution caused the Serb people to basically experience a death. If you have one constituent people in a country that had -- had this status over centuries, then what happened subsequently to the people is without precedent in history. I'm a historian. I can tell you that. Where you have a nation which is a constituent nation and had been back in the 16th, 17th century, all through to the 20th century, the only precedent was the Ustasha state in the 1941 to 1945 period. And this is the actual cause of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, that was quite a long answer, and I'm -- please, I want you to really focus on just answering my questions and try to keep it brief, if you can. And my question was -- I guess maybe it wasn't clear. I'm focused on the timing of the war, and you say that before this -- these changes to the constitution there is no war, no one was thinking of war. There's an exhibit in our case, Exhibit 491. I can show it to you if you want to, but I don't think we need to pull it up. And what it is is it's an official decision by the RSK on the 28th of July, 1992, that they decided -- they officially determined that the war started on the 17th of August, 1990. Were you aware of that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No decision was made concerning the war in -- having started in 1990. It could only have been done by Milan Babic to have issued a declaration of the state of war, but nobody accepted this. And this was done outside the Croatian -- the Serb National Council. The war actually started on the 31st of March, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with the well-known events at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see on the e-court, please, Exhibit 491. I think we'll have to turn to the second page in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, can you see there that this is a document from the RSK and it's dated the 28th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down, please. There, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you see there in numbered paragraph 1 that it says that the war began on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is on page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it should be. I didn't bring a hard copy, but it should be on page 2 of the English and the B/C/S. The B/C/S is on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I have the English. I have the English on my screen, and there's no sentence on ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that Zdravko Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so that we can all follow along with you. I apologise for the interruption. Just a moment

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I've got on my screen. I've got military post number 6065, internal number 234-1, 28th of August, 1992, Petrinje. And then from there it's all blank right down up to the bottom where it just says page 2. Unless -- unless I've got a completely different -- okay, it has come on my screen now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour, I'm glad we sorted that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, first before you give your explanation it's correct here that it says here that according to the RSK the war started on the 17th of August, 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right. Your Honours, it's not right that the war began on that date --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, sorry, let me interrupt you fist. But this was -- that was the conclusion of the RSK, correct, and I'll give you a chance to explain why you disagree, but it says here that the war started on the 17th of August, 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a document by the president, President Zecevic. He's a man who runs ahead of the cart sometimes. But the war didn't begin then, it began in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, by -- by blaming the December 1990 constitution for causing the war, what you're really trying to do is shift all the blame away from any Serbs and push all that blame on to Croatia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to object -- just a minute, sir. I have an objection to make over the observation in the sentence that the blame should be put on the other side. Does the Prosecutor wish to try the Serbs in this trial? In the transcript it says "Serbs," but the translation we got was the Serb people. So what I'm objecting to is this: I'm objecting to the position taken by the Prosecution and his question. Is he trying to shift the blame from the Serb people to the other side? That is quite unacceptable, or perhaps the Prosecutor thinks otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a baseless objection. What I said was is the witness trying to shift the blame away from any Serbs, those were the words I used, any Serbs and put the blame on to Croatia? The Serbs or the Serb people obviously are not on trial here; Milan Martic is. But what I'm focused on is what the witness is trying to do in his statement by shifting all blame on to Croatia and away from any Serb actors, be it the RSK or individual Serbs or any Serbs. That is why I used that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness can be right or can be mistaken when he tries, as the Prosecutor says, to shift the blame to the Croatian state. But to say that it is the people who are to blame, to formulate a question in that way is something that is quite unacceptable. And in this Tribunal we try cases on the principle of individual responsibility, each individual, each accused. There are no entire nations that were to blame; there were during World War II and they ended up in the crematoriums and in Jasinovac. We saw what that was like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you are not allowed to say something. The objection is overruled. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, do you need me to repeat the question or do you remember it, can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sure. Let me go back and try to make sure that I put it the same way. By blaming the December 1990 constitution for causing the war, what you're really trying to do is shift all the blame away from any Serbs and push all that blame on to Croatia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. The Serbs are a minority nation in Croatia and were never able to dictate to the majority Croatian population, or rather, its leadership what they were supposed to do and how they should function. So the Serbs in this case were the minority nation and the victims. And I say with full responsibility that this constitution, the so-called Christmas constitution, was at the centre and was, in fact, the basis of the war in Croatia. Had that constitution not existed, had we remained a constituent people in Croatia, I say with full responsibility as a historian there would have been no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn your attention now to paragraphs 29 and 30 of your statement, where you refer to dismissals of Serbs and in particular you talk about loyalty oaths. Isn't it true, sir, that some Croats were also forced to declare loyalty or be removed from their jobs in the SAO Krajina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such cases, although -- well, I don't know about them personally, but I could have heard stories to the effect that Croats that opposed the HDZ policy also had to bear the blame and make declarations and statements. However, I don't personally know about that, although I did hear about cases of that kind happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm -- maybe my question wasn't clear. What I meant to ask you about is that in 1991 some Croats were forced to sign or declare their loyalty to the SAO Krajina or risk being removed from their jobs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really answer that question. All I know is what the rumours were, that there were Croats who had to write declarations and things of that kind, but those were rare cases. I named two people from Zagreb whom I knew who worked in the defence ministry and who one day some 20 of them were called to a meeting and they were told that they were not going to work after that day. In my firm where I was the director, there were 37 employees and an order arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- according to which we were supposed to dismiss --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you talking about Croats being dismissed from their jobs within the SAO Krajina or are you talking about something different than that now?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing about the dismissal of Croats in SAO Krajina. I'm talking about the Serbs being let go en masse from their jobs throughout the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, that's in your statement, and I was asking you about something -- specifically about Croats being dismissed and I think you said you didn't know anything about that. Let me give you one specific instance and see if that jogs your memory; if it doesn't, just tell us. It's true, isn't it, that in early 1991 ethnic Croat police in Plaski were required to sign loyalty oaths to the SAO Krajina MUP or they were dismissed, isn't that right, or do you not know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn your attention to paragraph -- well, in fact it's mentioned in paragraph 31, paragraph 33, 38, paragraph 54 and maybe others, and the topic is illegal arming, and you make a number of references to illegal arming by Croatia. And my first question on this topic, sir, is: Isn't it true that Serbs in the Krajina were also illegally arming themselves from August 1990 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that weapons at the time were being procured in one way or another because evil times were looming and people came by those weapons on the black market mostly clandestinely. You would give your cow for one rifle and things of that kind; that's what people did. But there was no systematic arming in 1990. Some weapons from the JNA or other sources or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, okay, I think there's two things. First, it wasn't a hundred per cent clear, but do I take you to say: Yes, Serbs were illegally arming themselves in the Krajina from 1990 -- August 1990 onwards? And then I'll move to the question of organisation afterwards. But could we get a clear answer to that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were sporadic cases whereby people purchased weapons, but it wasn't on a massive scale until Croatia threw us out, or rather, the leadership threw us out of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "people," just so that it's a hundred per cent clear, you're talking about Serb people, people of Serb ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in fact, that arming was organised, I would put to you, by people including Milan Martic and the Council for National Resistance, for example, there was organised arming of Serbs from August 1990 onwards, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the arming started mostly in 1991. I don't know about that happening in 1990, any systematic arming at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But would you agree with me that certainly in 1991 there was systematic arming of the Serbs, Serb population in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not then, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When -- when do you say that this systematic arming began?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see. I was the president of a party, and I was the vice-president of the Serbian National Council. I was not in that sphere and didn't have contacts of that kind, so I can't really say when it began. And it's been 11 years since then. I am a refugee. I haven't been back to my native area and 15 or 16 years have elapsed since those events, so I can't remember now. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about something very specific and it happened either in July or of August of 1991. You personally transported a truckload of weapons sent by Milan Martic through Bosnia up to the Petrova Gora region, right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what year that was. I can't tell you that now, but I know that there was some trophy weapon -- there was some trophy weapons in a truck and that we transported it, but not to attack Croatia, to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And on that trip do you remember running into Milan Babic and talking to him?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not during that trip. All I know is that I met Milan Babic somewhere in the area of Novi, but that wasn't at that time. It was on another occasion when we had this meeting in a motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And on that occasion, when you met Milan Babic in the area of Novi, at that time you were also transporting a truckload of weapons, weren't you, sent by Milan Martic. And you were taking them back to Vojnic, to Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It wasn't then. In my opinion, that did not happen then, because we had a separate meeting with Milan Babic but that wasn't at the time when that truckload of weapons was being transported. I don't remember that that happened then. At that meeting Milan Babic put me forward as staff commander of the Territorial Defence, so commander of a -- the structure of a federal state, a legal structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I see, sir, I think we may be talking about two different events to some extent. And I'm focused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, before you proceed, I would just like to find out from the witness. The occasion that you're talking about in respect of the transportation of weapons that you were involved in, where were the weapons being transported from to, and about how many weapons were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the weapons were loaded up onto a truck; that was in Knin -- well, not really in Knin but the place near Knin - what was its name? - I'll remember in due course. It was trophy weapons, M-48 rifles, that kind of thing, of different calibres, but not combat weapons, not the kind of weapons that the Yugoslav People's Army used, but it was trophy weapons from a depot. I can't tell you how many. I remember there were 15 rifles of that kind and probably other weapons as well, but I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What precisely are trophy weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trophy weapons are old weapons, dating back to World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But these weapons, they would still have been in working order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, it could be used, yes, certainly. But it lagged far behind the other types of sophisticated weapons that were being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You have told us where the weapons were loaded, in Knin, but where was the destination, the final destination, for those weapons and did they reach there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did reach Petrova Gora, and it was stored up there. And the Territorial Defence had control of that weaponry. I don't know what happened to those weapons afterwards, myself. It was distributed to people who went to do village watches, part of the village guards, watching over their villages, not to attack anybody but to stand guard over their villages and to prevent an attack or crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, I'm going to move on to a new topic now, and it's at paragraph 33 of your statement. I guess it's actually -- it's still connected to the issue of arming but there specifically you talk about Martin Spegelj, and there's one phrase in particular. You say: "The whole Croatia backed Spegelj." Sir, that's a bit of an exaggeration, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it wasn't stated in the best way. We can't actually say that the whole of Croatia did, but most of the Croatian public. I don't want to say the people, but public figures in Croatia certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you say most of the Croatian public figures, I think is what you're saying, but it's also true, right, that there were public figures in Croatia who did not back Spegelj, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that in Martin Spegelj's published memoirs he describes how Tudjman, Franjo Tudjman, disagreed with him about the need to arm Croatia, that they had disputes about that issue? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that Spegelj was dismissed from his post as defence minister by Tudjman in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he left his post, but he was always in the -- those political and military circles. He was always someone to be reckoned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Look now at paragraphs 35 and to some extent -- yeah, 35 and 42, which talk about Plitvice. I want to ask you a couple questions about that. First of all, in paragraph 35 you say that in February 1991 the Croatian MUP established a police station in Plitvice where one had never existed before. Sir, Croatia, and specifically the Croatian MUP, was entitled to establish police stations anywhere on its territory; correct? There was nothing unlawful about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember those events. On that particular day, the 31st, I happened to be in Plaski, not far away from Plitvice --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, let me interrupt you. I think you're getting ahead of me a little bit. I want to ask you about this specific issue about --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's no problem. Before we get on to the 31st of March, you say that the Croatian MUP established a police station in Plitvice where one had never existed before. And my question is that it's correct, isn't it, that the Croatian MUP was entitled to establish police stations anywhere on its territory; there was nothing unlawful about that.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it was lawful or not, I don't know, but -- well, that's a debatable point. Whether at -- during those fateful days in a purely Serb area where the Serbs made 90 per cent of the population in the Plitvice area, whether it was opportune to set up a police station there. The Serbs saw that as a threat and, quite simply, did not agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just -- I'm sorry to do this to you. From -- from your question, Mr. Black, I inferred that the word "redarstvenici" means MUP. I just want to get confirmation of meaning of that word. "Redarstvenici," Witness, what does that word mean? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me? Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed it is a question for you, sir. It's a word from your statement; I want to know what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question. Do you mean the secretary or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not meaning the secretary. I'm meaning that word that is written in paragraph 35 that's in italics that reads "redarstvenici," or I don't know whether I'm pronouncing it correctly. I just want to know what that word means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "redarstvenici" were policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that policemen or is that MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, members of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, that's -- they were under the control or command of the MUP of Croatia, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, it's also true, isn't it, that the SAO Krajina police established police stations where none had ever existed before in different places, including, for example, Civljani, isn't that right, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. That's -- if you don't -- if you don't know about that, that's fine. I can move on to the next question. Let's look now a little bit at paragraph 42 and together with paragraph 35. In paragraph 42, you say that the Croatian special forces attacked Serbian villages and village guards in order to re-establish their police station in Plitvice on the 31st of March, 1991. And I'm a little confused because in paragraph 35 you said that a police station was set up in February, and now you're saying that they were trying to re-establish one at the end of March. And those two don't seem to go together. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain it in this way. There were attempts to establish it for the first time, to establish a police station for the first time, but there was intervention from the Yugoslav People's Army on that occasion. And I think that that police station withdrew, so this was a second attempt to establish a police station at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned the Yugoslav People's Army, but in paragraph 35 you say that SUP Secretary Martic was the one that asked the Croatian MUP to leave Plitvice. Was it Martic or was it the JNA, or both?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both. Both. Martic asked that that be done, as far as I remember, and so did the SFRY Presidency, to avoid a war, to avoid a conflict, and to calm the situation down, to prevent a war from breaking okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and -- so that request was essentially honoured, and in February 1991 a police station was not -- not established in Plitvice, just so I have the chronology right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember -- I knew it existed for quite some time after the -- I see, on February, you're asking me about February. No, I don't think it existed; that's my opinion at least, that it wasn't in existence in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for going a couple minutes over. It's a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's okay. And the Chamber has received word that the problem that we had with -- the technical problem that we had this morning that caused us to start late still persists and that they will need 45 minutes to sort it out. So we will take a break and come back at 11.00 instead of quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are sorry about these technological problems, but what can we do. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, just before our break we were talking a bit about Plitvice, which you describe what happened on the 31st of March, 1991, in paragraph 42 of your statement. And, sir, I put to you that you account here distorts what really happened, which was that the SAO Krajina police provoked the fighting at Plitvice, and specifically they went to Plitvice and they took up combat positions which provoked a response from the Croatian special police and that's how the fighting started. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. This is an area inhabited exclusively by Serbs, and the Serb people didn't allow the police station to be set up. And none of the Serbs attacked the Croatian police on their way to Plitvice. They simply did not allow them to gain entrance to Plitvice. So it wasn't the case that the Serb people started the violence first; it was the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Again -- and I don't know if -- what leads to this confusion, but I'm not talking about necessarily the Serb people, I'm talking about the Serb police, the SAO Krajina police, just so that's clear. And what I'm putting to you, sir, is that it was the SAO Krajina police who provoked this conflict by taking up combat positions in and around Plitvice. Am I right that you -- do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that because the side which is in the position to defend one's own area is not the one attacking. The question is: Why did Croatia insist so much on setting up a Croatian police station in an area inhabited exclusively by Serbs? It is known who arrived in the area and attacked the other side. We know that the Serbian people did not attack anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I think I can move on to the next topic. Please look at paragraph 40 of your statement. And there you say that from the 16th of May, 1991, onwards "all" --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: "All power was concentrated in the hands of Milan Babic." And, sir, in fact isn't it the case that although Milan Babic was certainly a powerful political figure in the Krajina in 1991, Milan Martic was an even more powerful figure, particularly with regard to operational matters; things like the arming of the population, the functioning of the police, and particularly the formation, training and arming of the police special purpose units. And in all those operational fields, Milan Martic was much more influential than was Milan Babic. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this can't be the case. Milan Martic was a clerk, an administrator in the SAO government, in the SAO Krajina government. He was far below Milan Babic -- well, he may have out-topped Babic in terms of popularity, the press coverage he received and so on and so forth. However, Milan Babic was the political figure at the head of the SAO Krajina leadership, whereas Milan Babic [as interpreted] was simply an administrator working for the SAO Krajina at the post of the minister of the interior. There was a harmony existing between Milan Babic and Milan Martic up until the end of May - now which year was it? -- 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. There's one point of confusion just in the translation, I think, or maybe you misspoke but I think it's clear from your answer in total. You're saying that Milan Martic was a clerk, or an administrator, in the SAO government, although there's a -- on page 27, line 10 -- excuse me, line 11 there is reference to Milan Babic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But I think that was a mistake, and it's clear from the record, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you say he was a clerk or an administrator. He was the minister of the interior, right? That's not a low-level position.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Compared to Milan Babic, who was the president of the SAO Krajina, that is the case, because the two roles are not comparable. Milan Babic was the leading figure and he was the mover and shaker at the time. He made a lot of mistakes and did many things that were detrimental for our people. However, when gauging the two persons, the popularity was more or less the same. However, Babic was above Milan Martic, who was a minister, a member of the Krajina cabinet. A minister, in my view, is simply a -- a clerk, an administrator working for the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness, but you do accept that Mr. Martic was the minister of the interior at the time that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, both according -- according to the law -- and actually -- and according to reality, Milan Martic was in control of all Krajina police from -- from early on, certainly from the end -- or certainly no later than the beginning of 1991 onward. He was always in control of the police, Mr. Milan Martic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was at the head of the police force and he controlled the police force as far as one was able to, given the turbulent times, the war broke out, and it was a dirty war. Therefore, to the extent one was able to firmly -- have a firm grasp over matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me move you to another topic. At paragraph 43 of your statement you refer to a decision in April 1991 to hold a referendum on annexing Krajina to Serbia. And you call this a "fatal decision for the Serb people," which you blame on Milan Babic. And here's my question, sir: Isn't it correct that Milan Babic's mistake was that -- simply that he spoke too openly or acted too openly about the goal of unifying Serb lands? He was too open about that; whereas Mr. Milosevic and other Serb leaders would have preferred that that be discussed only privately and that the public focus be on preserving Yugoslavia. Is what I've said accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the heart of these affairs, and we had a meeting in Korenica of the Serbian National Council. And Milan Babic, as the president, proposed that we schedule a referendum. The Serbian National Council opposed the idea and I myself stated that we should by no means take that direction, that we should try to find our place in Croatia. By acting this way, we would give leeway to the other side to take the steps that they wanted to. Unfortunately, Milan Babic insisted on this but didn't go through the Serb National Council; rather, he went to the Association of Serb Municipalities. And in fact, on the 12th of May, 1991, the referendum was held. This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this dealt a great blow to the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I think all that was contained in your statement. To the extent you can, you don't -- it's not really necessary to repeat what's in the statement because it's in evidence, but thanks for your explanation. And the real point of my question is that, you know, you say that by acting in this way you would give leeway to the other side to take the steps that they wanted to. And that was my point. It wasn't a problem of substance, this idea of unifying all Serbs in one unified state; it was the fact that if you talked about it openly, that caused problems with the international community or it gave a justification to Croatia for their actions. That was the real problem, right, it was about openly addressing this issue. It wasn't a question of substance on unifying all Serbs in one state.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, as much as the Croatian people had the right to set up their own state, and they have to take credit for that, for the fact that they managed to set up their own state, the other equal nation in Croatia had the same right to pursue their own course, their right of self-determination. However, the referendum was detrimental to our side, given the time when it was held, and it caused a rift between Babic and Milosevic. And I'm sure that Milosevic did not back the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And let me just ask this one more time and see if I can get clarity on this. The reason that Milosevic, for instance, did not back the referendum was not that Milosevic didn't want Krajina and Serbia to be united or for there to be Serbs united in a single state, the reason he didn't back it was because he thought that openly advocating this unification was going to cause problems with the international community and with Croatia, right? Is that correct, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speculate on what Milosevic's thoughts on this were, but I know for a fact that from that point on the relations between Milan Babic and Milosevic became troubled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Had the SAO Krajina's annexation to Serbia been successful and accepted by Serbia in May of 1991, that would have constituted the first change to the internal borders of Yugoslavia, wouldn't it? Because Croatia and Slovenia had not yet declared independence in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been only natural for all equal nations because the area was not merely divided into republics and provinces, but it was also a country of different nations. And therefore, it would have only been natural for all nations to decide what their fate would be. Therefore, the fact that the Serbs would leave Croatia would not be an unlawful move; it would be based on the basic postulates of justice and democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're getting away from my question. I'm not focused on the lawfulness. We've actually had other witnesses testify about these kinds of issues. But am I correct that in May 1991 had this annexation been accepted by Serbia, that would have been the first change to the internal borders of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allowed the witness to answer this question once, although it was a question asking for a speculative answer, what would have been the case had things happened this way or other way, and this is quite unacceptable because this isn't what happened. And the witness has already answered the same question. So this is calling for pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not calling for any speculation; I'm trying to emphasise a point of the time-line. It's a question of when things happened. You know, these were proposed changes to the borders in May 1991; later on there were declarations of independence in June of 1991. And I just wanted to get clear with the witness that that's the correct chronology and this would have been the first change. I don't think that's improperly speculative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this definitely calls for speculation because in the month of May Croatia held a referendum on the secession from Yugoslavia. The referendum resulted in the actual secession. So such a question could be put because this indeed happened. In this case it did not happen, and the Prosecutor asked what would have happened happened had this indeed been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand my question? It isn't -- I don't think it's -- it shouldn't be a controversial one. It's just this: Had the SAO Krajina's annexation to Serbia been accepted by Serbia in May 1991, that would have been the first change to the internal borders of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been the first. But it would have been a reasonable one because, as you know, under all the rules every constituent nation has the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you. We've had plenty of evidence about that and I wasn't really asking about whether it was reasonable or unreasonable. I just wanted to focus on the timing. Let me turn you to another topic, and you should look at paragraph 45 of your statement. There you say that Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in May 1991 in Trogir advocated riots against the JNA. Sir, you're referring to a speech in Trogir in early May that -- a speech that Tudjman gave in Trogir in early May; correct? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to the speech in Trogir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In that speech Tudjman said that he wondered why people were not demonstrating outside of barracks. He didn't call for violence or he didn't call for blockades of the barracks; he just wondered why people hadn't been demonstrating. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isn't that the same thing, Mr. Prosecutor? It's the same thing but differently worded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about that. I understood in your statement riots to mean violence, whereas you could presumably have a peaceful demonstration. So are you referring -- when you say that Tudjman called -- he advocated riots, are you talking about violent action or are you talking about peaceful action, demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, I'm speaking about acts of violence, because at the time the barracks were already under siege, their water and food supplies were cut off. This constitutes violence and not a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you say those things were already happening in May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not systematically, but what happened in Trogir and in Split and the victim, Sasa Petrovski and the -- Sasa Gesovski and the strangling of the soldier on a tank, these were no longer demonstrations; this was an event of quite a different nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And am I accurate - or perhaps you don't know - but isn't it correct that Tudjman did not call for violence, he didn't call for violent acts like that, he just wondered why people hadn't been demonstrating, which is slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any experienced politician would term it in these particular terms. A soldier or anybody else wouldn't know how to use terminology to serve one's own turn, but in actual fact the meaning was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're accepting that he didn't actually use these words. He didn't actually call for violence or riots. What he asked about was demonstrations, just focusing on the words that he used, you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the text of what he said. I recall the strong reaction in Krajina to his speech in Trogir. It augured ill for a country that was a recognised UN member state. Any other state would have acted in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't remember the words that he used, that's fine. Am I to understand that you don't really remember the words that he used?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the exact words. I remember the meaning, that it was irritating and it portended blockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You've explained that more than once now. Please look -- well, actually at the end of paragraph 45 you refer to signatures being collected, as you say, to forbid members of the SDS to stay in Sibenik. You're referring to a petition that had to do with Jovan Raskovic and a couple of other people, and that was -- it was signed in August of 1990, right? Is that the event you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that is the event. You had Branko Popovic testifying here; you could have asked him. He was directly threatened. Marko Dobrijevic is in Belgrade now. Jovan Raskovic is no more unfortunately. But I do recall that the signatures were collected and that they had to leave Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In fact, questions were put to Mr. Popovic on this, but you don't need to concern yourself with that. Do you remember what the petition actually said? Do you know if you read it or do you remember the actual language of the petition?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I knew the people involved very well, I socialised with them, we met frequently and discussed these matters, and therefore I knew what the petition meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you never saw the petition itself, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it. I know what I heard from them and the result of it all was that they were compelled to leave the area. But the petition evidently existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Since you haven't seen the petition -- well, let me ask -- let me just put this question to you. In fact, sir, the petition which is Exhibit -- the language is set out in 939, Exhibit 939, but I don't think we need to put it out on our screens unless you want to have a look at it. What it says is they were upset with these people and that they wished they weren't around, but it doesn't actually expel them or forbid them to stay in Sibenik, does it? Just focusing really on exactly what the petition said or called for. Do you accept what I've said or not? Or do you feel like you need to look at the document to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at the document, since I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. It's Exhibit 939. I'm just trying to keep us moving quickly because we do have a lot of ground to cover today, sir, but we can take a moment and look at this document on our screens hopefully. And, sir, the part that I'm interested in bears the title "Petition Against Representatives." Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Petition, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: "Petition against representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party in Sibenik." And I'm sorry that I can't -- I'm not much use to help you find it on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be there at the top. Yes, yes, now we can see it. "We would be happy if you were to disappear forever," and I believe that's the text referring to the petition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Defence counsel. Thank you for helping me out on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, maybe you'll find this to be an overly subtle point, but I just want to ask you: According to the text of this petition, and it says that they -- the people who signed the petition feel offended and humiliated, and even, it says, they would be happy if they disappeared forever from their environment, but it doesn't actually expel them. It doesn't actually say that they can't stay there, does it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this isn't the petition; this is a newspaper article. This piece of information was shaped by the journalist. I thought I was going to be presented with the actual petition. This doesn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, this is from the publication Politika. Are you saying that you think the petition actually was different than this, that this doesn't accurately represent the language of the petition?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Historians, we historians are quite stubborn when it comes to documents. This isn't a document, in my view; this is a -- an -- a work product.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So do you think that the petition was differently worded than this or do you simply not know? I think you said you hadn't seen it. If you don't know, that's fine and we can just move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've not seen the petition, but in my view this isn't the text of the petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I can take this any further with this witness given those answers, so I'll move on to the next topic, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Dakic, thank you. Please look at paragraph 52 and actually the paragraphs which follow in your statement. You mention a whole number of attacks and crimes allegedly committed by Croatian police and special forces against Serb forces and Serb civilians. My first question, sir: In 1991 there were also attacks by Serb forces, such as the SAO Krajina police, the TO, and the JNA against Croat villages, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were attacks, or rather, there were attacks from both sides. I can't deny the fact that there were crimes. You have crimes in all wars, on both sides. But I was the president of the state commission for war crimes, and I gathered information about them. Unfortunately -- well, I gathered information from both sides, who killed whom. But unfortunately they stayed in Knin during these -- Operation Storm and I'm very sorry about that. But anyway, I learned about this from various documents later on, what happened, where, in which area, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you accept that there were actually crimes committed by both sides and against civilians of both ethnicities, Serb and Croat; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I accept that, yes, that there were crimes on both sides, but on the majority side far more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how come you didn't mention any of these crimes by Serb forces in your statement? And doesn't it seem like you provided a very one-sided view in your statement. You only mention the crimes by one side and you haven't said anything about the crimes by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that all the documents was -- all the documents were left in Knin, and I recorded both sides. So that's a great misfortune that they stayed there, those documents and information. But in the statement I expose spoke about crimes committed by the majority side, that is to say the side that had absolutely no reason for destroying that peoples. And that nation is being destroyed to the present day through genocide and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, sir, let me interrupt you. Somehow you managed to remember about the crimes against Serbs, even though the documentation was left behind in Knin; how come you didn't remember or you didn't include crimes against Croats in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: I was far away from the front line. I was in the rear, and I followed what was going on through television, the press, and so on. I wasn't up at the front lines where the fighting was going on. So I didn't go where the shooting was done and where the killing was done, but later on I saw the results of that, of those crimes. And then I recorded it. And as I say, my documentation was left behind. And of course I had greater access to this one side where the Croats had stormed the area and committed crimes. I heard a lot about that. I heard a lot about Sisak, about Slavonia, and so on and so forth. But I maintained that there were crimes, of course, committed on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the people were not responsible for that on any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Am I to understand -- you say that you weren't at the front lines where the fighting was going on, you didn't go where the shooting was done and where the killing was done. Am I to take it that all the material you provide here about crimes by Croatian forces against Serb police, this is also stuff that you don't have personal knowledge about. You didn't -- you don't have direct knowledge about those things; you just have maybe what you read in the press or that you gleaned from other sources, but no personal knowledge about it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was it the Medak pocket, and immediately after the operation there I went and contacted UNPROFOR. I was in the delegation, in fact, and I saw what Jean-Claude said that there wasn't a single bird left alive, not life at all, let alone people. I saw that. That's what I saw. But otherwise I gathered the rest from documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. You also had access to documents, I take it, which discussed crimes by Serb forces against Croats or did you have no such access?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have access to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So how did you -- you said that there were crimes by the Serb forces; how did you learn about such crimes? And can you give us any specific examples of the kind of things you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see. I know that in different parts of Krajina the situation differed. For example, in the Dalmatian part there were a great deal of Croatian houses that had been destroyed, and I know that lots of things happened there. But it was only later on that I saw the extent of the evil perpetrated by Croatian forces against another nation; it was a complete nightmare. And it was difficult -- well, Tudjman himself said that he needed a war, and that's what happened. And please bear in mind the fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you. You keep focusing -- you keep sort of gliding back to what the Croatian forces did, and I just wanted to focus, just for this instance now, on Serb forces. Do you have any specific examples of crimes committed by Serb forces or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concrete examples, no, I do not have any concrete examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I heard about them, just like others did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your answer. Thank you. At paragraphs 59 and 60 at least, maybe 61, too, it's not clear to me, you refer specifically to crimes against Serbs in Western Slavonia in the fall of 1991. But I take it that you were not in Western Slavonia at that time, and so I take it you -- you don't -- this is one of the things where you don't have personal knowledge about those crimes; these are things you learned about through other means. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to crimes in Western Slavonia, Dr. Vojin Babic wrote a lot about that. And in his book you will find all the facts and figures of how 18 Serb villages were destroyed. It was the first mass ethnic cleansing of Serbs from Croatia, which happened at the end of 1991. And later on I went to a number of places in Eastern Slavonia, in Dalj, for instance, and I learned of the crime that took place in Dalj. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I'm just focusing on Western Slavonia for the time being, so please focus your answer just on Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did this book by Mr. Vojin Babic, did that also include evidence about crimes against Croats in Western Slavonia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dabic, Dabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Dabic. Did Mr. Dabic -- or did this book by Vojin Dabic, did that also include information about crimes against Croats in Western Slavonia in 1991, do you recall, or was it exclusively about Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a research worker. He is professor at the University of Belgrade, and he published this book, and I used the book to learn about what happened in Western Slavonia. And I'm sure you know the exodus that took place, the exodus of the Serbs in -- from Western Slavonia at the end of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Vojin Dabic treats both sides equally; he doesn't spare either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that yes, indeed, his book includes information on crimes against Croats in Western Slavonia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, how come you didn't mention --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mention it because the crimes in Western Slavonia against Croats is something that -- or, rather, Vojin Dabic gave intimations that there were crimes on both sides. However, what happened to the Serbs in Western Slavonia cannot be compared at all to what happened to the Croats, because the Serbs were completely ethnically cleansed from 18 villages. That was the first instance of mass ethnic cleansing, and it was the Serbs who were the victims in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that in Vocin Croats civilians were mistreated and harassed from August of 1991 until December, and in December 1991 more than 40 Croat civilians were massacred in Vocin. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Vocin in 1990. I didn't know about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew many people, but -- no, I did not know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that between the summer and October of 1991 Croats were killed in Donji Cavlic [phoen], Cetekovac, Balinci, Bacin and Bujice [phoen]. I apologise if I'm not pronouncing those names exactly right. But did you know about Croats being killed in those places at that time in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that Croat civilians were detained in detention facilities and mistreated in Bujice and in Stara Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- let me focus your attention on paragraph 61, where you say that 141.000 Serbs were expelled from Croatian towns where there was no combat. Sir, what time-frame are you referring to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the entire time-frame during the war. There are exact -- there is exact information pertaining to refugees in Serbia, and a list from -- of refugees from 1996 that says who came from what area, what refugee came from what area, where they live, and so on. And then I conducted research on that basis. And 141.887 Serbs were expelled from Croatian towns where there was no war. That's the heart of the matter. They were expelled not because they expressed themselves against the leadership. Now, why were 5.100 Serbs expelled from Rijeka? Why were several hundred Serbs expelled from Pula, from Varazdin, from Zagreb, where there was no war and so on and so forth. And that is the greatest blow to the Serb people in Croatia because they were -- it was the Serb intelligentsia that was expelled from the towns, and a nation without its intelligentsia is a maimed nation and cannot continue to live, and their citizens' rights have been taken away from them so they are not able to return today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you're getting a little bit away from my question, but thank you for your answer. You mentioned a -- I'm not exactly clear, could you specify what your source is for this number? I think you referred to it in your answer but I didn't quite get it, the source you used to arrive at this number.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source is the refugees census or list of refugees in Serbia and Montenegro conducted in 1996, and they are just -- it just includes people from Serbia and Montenegro -- in Serbia and Montenegro, but how many were expelled to Republika Srpska, to America, and to other western countries is a far larger number of Serbs expelled from Croatian towns where there was no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, actually, while you say that I just -- isn't it correct that -- that even this number, 141.000, that's exaggerated. The numbers were actually significantly smaller than that, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, far greater. The figure is far greater. Because this just refers to those that arrived on the territory Serbia and Montenegro, whereas the others are not included on that list. So quite certainly we have another 20.000 to 30.000 people who were expelled from Croatian towns. The exact figure is what I tell you because I published it in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when did you provide this figure to the Defence; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
